lead.en: An armistice fixes a divided peninsula

summary.en: In June 1950 North Korean troops crossed the 38th parallel. UN forces led by the US fought for the South, Chinese volunteers backed by the USSR for the North. The 1953 armistice at Panmunjom fixed the division of Korea that endures today.

lead.en: A record Maracanã crowd falls silent as Uruguay wins the Cup

summary.en: On 16 July 1950 Brazil needed only a draw in the deciding World Cup match. The Maracanã held 173,850 paying fans, an all-time record, and perhaps 220,000 in all. Uruguay won 2–1, and Brazil later ditched its 'unpatriotic' white kit for yellow and green.

lead.en: Coal smoke chokes the capital and leads to a Clean Air Act

summary.en: From 5 to 9 December 1952 still air trapped coal smoke over London, cutting visibility to a few metres. Later estimates put the death toll at up to 10,000–12,000. The disaster led to the Clean Air Act of 1956, in the first year of Elizabeth II's reign.

title.en: European bison return to the wild

lead.en: A species saved only in captivity roams Białowieża again

summary.en: The last wild bison of Białowieża was shot in 1921 and the last Caucasian one in 1927, leaving the species only in zoos and estates. Breeders rebuilt the herd from a few dozen animals, and in 1952 the first bison were released into Białowieża Forest.

title.en: Discovery of the DNA double helix

lead.en: Watson and Crick's model explains how heredity works

summary.en: In April 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick published their double-helix model of DNA in Nature, drawing on X-ray images by Rosalind Franklin. It revealed how heredity works and gave birth to molecular biology.

lead.en: Hillary and Tenzing on the roof of the world

summary.en: On 29 May 1953 the New Zealander Edmund Hillary and the Sherpa Tenzing Norgay of John Hunt's British expedition became the first to stand on the world's highest summit. They spent about fifteen minutes on top; Tenzing left offerings to the gods in the snow. The news reached London on the day of Elizabeth II's coronation.

lead.en: The ruler of three decades dies, opening a struggle for power

summary.en: Joseph Stalin, who had led the USSR for about 30 years, died at his Kuntsevo dacha on 5 March 1953. An amnesty and the end of the 'Doctors' plot' case soon followed, and a power struggle in the leadership was won by Khrushchev.

lead.en: Oil, the CIA and the roots of Iran's 1979 revolution

summary.en: In 1951 Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh nationalised the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. On 19 August 1953 he was overthrown by royalist army officers in a coup organised and funded by the CIA and Britain's MI6 — a role the US formally acknowledged in 2013. Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi consolidated personal rule, and memories of the coup fed the anti-Western mood of the 1979 revolution.

lead.en: Guns hauled up mountains by hand end an empire in Asia

summary.en: The French command built a fortified camp in a mountain valley, convinced the enemy could not bring artillery there. General Võ Nguyên Giáp's Viet Minh hauled guns up the surrounding slopes by hand. After a 56-day siege the garrison surrendered on 7 May 1954. France left Indochina, and the Geneva Conference divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel.

title.en: The Castle Bravo test at Bikini

lead.en: Expected 6 megatons, got 15 and radioactive snow

summary.en: On 1 March 1954 the US detonated a thermonuclear device at Bikini: a calculation error made it 15 megatons instead of the expected six, the largest American explosion ever. White radioactive ash fell on Rongelap Atoll and on the Japanese fishing boat Lucky Dragon No. 5, whose radio operator later died. Bikini's own people had been moved off in 1946; those who returned in the 1970s were evacuated again in 1978.

lead.en: A fight for independence topples France's Fourth Republic

summary.en: On 1 November 1954 the National Liberation Front launched an armed struggle against French rule. The brutal war divided French society and brought down the Fourth Republic. Under the 1962 Évian Accords Algeria became independent.

title.en: Obninsk, the first grid-connected nuclear power plant

lead.en: The atom feeds an industrial power grid for the first time

summary.en: In June 1954 the 5 MW Obninsk nuclear power plant was connected to the grid, becoming the world's first nuclear reactor to supply electricity to a power network. It operated until 2002.

lead.en: A doctor hit 1,000 km/h and stopped in about a second

place.en: Holloman Air Force Base, New Mexico

summary.en: Air Force doctor John Stapp tested on himself how much deceleration a human can take. On 10 December 1954 a rocket sled took him to 1,017 km/h and stopped him in 1.4 seconds; he survived 46 g, and his work fed into car seat belts.

lead.en: A long Cold War conflict ends with the fall of Saigon

summary.en: The war between North Vietnam, backed by the USSR and China, and South Vietnam, backed above all by the United States, was one of the longest conflicts of the Cold War. US troops left in 1973, and in 1975 Saigon fell and the country was reunified.

lead.en: Trials prove it works — polio begins to retreat

summary.en: On 12 April 1955 the results of huge field trials showed Jonas Salk's polio vaccine to be safe and effective. Together with Albert Sabin's oral vaccine, mass-tested in the USSR, it has nearly eradicated polio worldwide.

lead.en: Former colonies speak to the world on their own terms

summary.en: In April 1955 delegates from 29 Asian and African countries, most of them recently freed from colonial rule, met in Bandung. Among them were Sukarno, Nehru, Zhou Enlai and Nasser. The conference adopted ten principles of peaceful coexistence and condemned colonialism; the Non-Aligned Movement grew out of it.

lead.en: The Eastern Bloc forms a military alliance to counter NATO

summary.en: On 14 May 1955 the USSR and the socialist states of Eastern Europe signed a treaty of friendship, cooperation and mutual assistance in Warsaw. The military alliance stood opposite NATO until it was dissolved in 1991.

title.en: Secret Speech and the Khrushchev thaw

lead.en: Khrushchev denounces Stalin and Gulag prisoners are rehabilitated

summary.en: On 25 February 1956, at the 20th Party Congress, Nikita Khrushchev denounced Stalin's personality cult in a closed session. Mass rehabilitation of Gulag prisoners and a relaxation of censorship followed, known as the Thaw.

lead.en: Budapest moves to leave the bloc; Soviet troops crush the revolt

summary.en: On 23 October 1956 a student demonstration in Budapest grew into a revolt, and Imre Nagy's government announced withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact. Soviet troops crushed it from 4 November; about 2,500 Hungarians died and 200,000 fled.

lead.en: Nasser seizes the canal, and Britain's superpower days end

summary.en: On 26 July 1956 Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal. In late October Israel, Britain and France, acting on a secret pact, attacked Egypt and landed troops at Port Said. But the US and USSR demanded an end to the war, and the invaders had to withdraw. Nasser became a hero of the Arab world, British Prime Minister Eden resigned, and the UN deployed its first peacekeeping force.

lead.en: A Dartmouth seminar names the science of thinking machines

summary.en: In summer 1956 John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky and others gathered at Dartmouth College to explore thinking machines. The term 'artificial intelligence', coined by McCarthy for the proposal, gave the new field its name.

lead.en: The USSR opens the space age

summary.en: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union put the first artificial Earth satellite into orbit, its radio beeps picked up around the world. The launch opened the Space Age and started the space race between the USSR and the United States.

lead.en: Six nations launch a common market, the core of the future EU

summary.en: France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg signed in Rome the treaty creating the European Economic Community and its common market. It became the core of the future European Union.

lead.en: First in sub-Saharan Africa to end colonial rule

summary.en: The British colony of the Gold Coast, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became independent Ghana, the first sub-Saharan African country to throw off colonial rule. Its example inspired the decolonisation of the continent.

lead.en: The BBC shows a Swiss family harvesting spaghetti from trees

summary.en: On 1 April 1957 the BBC's serious current-affairs show Panorama ran a three-minute report on a Swiss family harvesting spaghetti from trees. Pasta was exotic in Britain then, and many viewers called to ask how to grow one. CNN later called it the biggest hoax ever pulled by a reputable news outlet.

lead.en: A Moscow street dog becomes the first animal in orbit

summary.en: On 3 November 1957, a month after the first Sputnik, Sputnik 2 carried the dog Laika, the first animal in Earth orbit. No return was planned; only in 2002 did a scientist on the project reveal that she had died of overheating within hours of launch.

lead.en: Colonialism through African eyes: Africa's defining novel

summary.en: In 1958 Chinua Achebe, a 27-year-old at the Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation, published a novel about Okonkwo, a proud Igbo strongman whose world collapses with the arrival of missionaries and British rule. He took the title from a poem by Yeats. The book has sold more than 20 million copies in dozens of languages and became the starting point of modern African literature.

lead.en: Mao's rush to industrialise brings a catastrophic famine

summary.en: In 1958 Mao Zedong launched the Great Leap Forward: peasants were herded into people's communes and millions smelted steel in backyard furnaces. Impossible targets and inflated harvest reports led to the famine of 1959–1961, which killed between 15 and 45 million people by various estimates.

lead.en: Whispered samba that conquered the world

summary.en: In 1958 guitarist João Gilberto recorded 'Chega de Saudade' by Antônio Carlos Jobim and Vinícius de Moraes, with a hushed voice and an unfamiliar guitar rhythm. Bossa nova, a blend of samba and cool jazz, was born. 'The Girl from Ipanema' became one of the most recorded songs ever, and the album Getz/Gilberto won the Grammy for Album of the Year.

lead.en: A bankrupt 48-year-old invents instant ramen

summary.en: Momofuku Ando had lost his company and was starting over with a small family firm in Ikeda. After months of trials he hit on flash-frying cooked noodles, and on 25 August 1958, aged 48, launched the first instant noodles, Chikin Ramen. He lived to 96 and said he ate them almost every day.

lead.en: The lemming 'suicide' was staged by filmmakers

summary.en: Disney's documentary showed lemmings hurling themselves into the sea, and it won an Oscar in 1959. It later emerged that the animals were filmed in landlocked Alberta, where they do not live, and were pushed off the cliff by the crew.

lead.en: Castro ousts Batista and the island allies with the USSR

summary.en: Guerrillas led by Fidel Castro and Che Guevara overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista, who fled on 1 January 1959; within days the rebels entered Havana. Cuba became the first socialist state in the Western Hemisphere and a Soviet ally off the US coast.

lead.en: A whole continent declared a zone of peace and science

summary.en: On 1 December 1959 in Washington, twelve nations, including the USSR and the US at the height of the Cold War, signed the Antarctic Treaty. It banned military bases, manoeuvres and nuclear explosions there, froze territorial claims and opened the continent to free scientific research. The 1991 Madrid Protocol added a ban on mining. More than 50 countries are now parties to it.

title.en: Tibetan uprising and the Dalai Lama's flight

lead.en: The Dalai Lama flees to India; Tibet becomes a global issue

summary.en: On 10 March 1959 thousands of Lhasa residents surrounded the Norbulingka palace, fearing Chinese authorities would detain the Dalai Lama. On 17 March he secretly fled, crossing into India at the end of the month; tens of thousands of Tibetans followed. The People's Liberation Army crushed the uprising; the death toll remains disputed. Beijing calls it a rebellion by the feudal elite, Tibetan exiles a national uprising.

lead.en: The Cold War fought over dishwashers and washing machines

summary.en: On 24 July 1959, at the American exhibition in Sokolniki Park, Vice President Nixon and Khrushchev argued capitalism versus communism beside the kitchen of a model US house cut in half for visitors. Recorded on colour videotape, the exchange was shown in both countries.

lead.en: Seventeen nations win independence in a single year

summary.en: In 1960 seventeen African countries gained independence, including Nigeria, Congo and most of France's colonies. The year marked the climax of the continent's decolonisation and sharply changed the make-up of the United Nations.

lead.en: The strongest quake ever measured sends waves across the Pacific

summary.en: On 22 May 1960 southern Chile was struck by the most powerful earthquake ever recorded, magnitude 9.5. Its tsunami crossed the Pacific, hitting Hawaii and Japan within a day. Two days later, the Cordón Caulle volcano began to erupt.

lead.en: A plane-shaped capital raised in the savanna in four years

summary.en: President Juscelino Kubitschek promised 'fifty years of progress in five' and moved the capital from the coast to the empty interior. The city, laid out by Lúcio Costa in a plan resembling a plane with outspread wings and filled with Oscar Niemeyer's buildings, was built in under four years. Brasília became the capital on 21 April 1960 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

title.en: Abebe Bikila wins the marathon barefoot

lead.en: Ethiopian guardsman runs the Olympic marathon barefoot and wins

summary.en: New shoes bought in Rome gave Abebe Bikila blisters, so on 10 September 1960 he ran the Olympic marathon barefoot. The imperial guardsman finished first by the Arch of Constantine in world-record time, Ethiopia's first Olympic champion. Four years later in Tokyo he won again, this time in shoes.

lead.en: Two men descend nearly 11 km to the bottom of the ocean

summary.en: On 23 January 1960 the bathyscaphe Trieste, carrying Swiss Jacques Piccard and American Don Walsh, reached the floor of the Challenger Deep at about 10,916 m. It was designed by the pilot's father, Auguste Piccard. No one went back for 52 years, until director James Cameron in 2012.

title.en: Belka and Strelka return from orbit

lead.en: Two dogs become the first living beings back from orbit

summary.en: On 19 August 1960 a spacecraft carried the dogs Belka and Strelka, 40 mice, two rats and plants into orbit. A day later all returned alive, a first. Less than eight months later Gagarin followed them, and Khrushchev gave Strelka's puppy Pushinka to the Kennedys.

lead.en: The first human in space circles the Earth

summary.en: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin aboard Vostok 1 became the first human in space. Circling the Earth once in 108 minutes, he landed safely in the Saratov region. The flight was a triumph for the Soviet space programme.

lead.en: A city is cut in two overnight — the Cold War made concrete

summary.en: On the night of 13 August 1961 East Germany sealed the border with West Berlin with barbed wire, later a concrete wall. It stopped the exodus of its citizens to the West and stood until 1989.

lead.en: Thirteen days on the brink of nuclear war

summary.en: In October 1962 the US discovered Soviet missiles in Cuba and imposed a naval quarantine. For thirteen days the world stood on the brink of nuclear war until Khrushchev and Kennedy agreed: the USSR removed its missiles, the US pledged not to invade Cuba and withdrew missiles from Turkey.

lead.en: Samoa opens the era of Pacific decolonisation

summary.en: On 1 January 1962 Western Samoa, administered by New Zealand as a UN trust territory, became the first Pacific Island nation to win independence, after decades of the non-violent Mau movement. Nauru (1968), Fiji (1970), Papua New Guinea (1975), the Solomon Islands (1978), Vanuatu (1980) and others followed.

lead.en: Troops fire on workers protesting against price rises

summary.en: In June 1962 workers at the locomotive plant went on strike after meat and butter prices were raised just as their pay rates were cut. On 2 June troops fired on the demonstration outside the party offices, killing 26; seven more were later executed. It stayed hushed up until 1989.

lead.en: Fits of laughter shut down 14 schools

summary.en: In early 1962 pupils at a girls' school in the village of Kashasha by Lake Victoria began laughing and crying uncontrollably. The mass hysteria spread to nearby villages and schools and died down only after 18 months. Some 1,000 people were affected and 14 schools had to close.

title.en: The Organisation of African Unity is founded

lead.en: The Pan-African dream takes shape; 25 May becomes Africa Day

summary.en: On 25 May 1963 leaders of 32 independent African states signed the charter of the Organisation of African Unity in Addis Ababa. Kwame Nkrumah called for a single African government, but most chose a union of sovereign states pledged to finish off colonialism and apartheid. The founding date is celebrated as Africa Day, and in 2002 the OAU was replaced by the African Union.

lead.en: Martin Luther King delivers "I Have a Dream"

summary.en: On 28 August 1963 some 250,000 people gathered in Washington for African American civil rights. At the Lincoln Memorial Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech. A year later the US passed the Civil Rights Act.

lead.en: The first woman in space orbits Earth 48 times

summary.en: On 16 June 1963 Vostok 6 lifted off from Baikonur with Valentina Tereshkova aboard. She became the first woman in space, orbiting the Earth 48 times in almost three days.

lead.en: An album cut in a day sets off Beatlemania

summary.en: In March 1963 the Liverpool quartet released their debut album, recorded at Abbey Road in a single day. Beatlemania followed, and the Beatles went on to transform popular music and youth culture worldwide.

lead.en: The 'red telephone' was never a telephone

summary.en: After the Cuban Missile Crisis the USSR and USA agreed on a direct link, which went live on 30 August 1963. Contrary to films it was no red phone but a teletype, later a fax. Washington's first message was the pangram about the quick brown fox and the lazy dog, to test every letter.

lead.en: Tokyo to Osaka at 210 km/h — the first high-speed line

summary.en: On 1 October 1964, just before the Olympics, the Tokyo–Osaka Shinkansen opened with trains running at up to 210 km/h. It was the world's first high-speed railway and a symbol of Japan's post-war revival.

lead.en: Asia's first Games show the world a renewed Japan

summary.en: In October 1964 Tokyo hosted the first Olympic Games held in Asia. The Games, the first relayed live by satellite, showcased a rebuilt Japan; the flame was lit by a young man born in Hiroshima on the day of the atomic bombing.

lead.en: His suit ballooned, then they landed in wolf-ridden taiga

summary.en: On 18 March 1965 Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, lasting 12 minutes. His suit ballooned and he got back into the airlock only by bleeding its pressure below safe limits. The capsule landed off target in taiga near Perm, and the crew spent two freezing nights there with a pistol against wolves and bears.

lead.en: A decade of purges, Red Guards and smashed heritage

summary.en: In May 1966 Mao Zedong declared war on 'bourgeois elements' in the party and society. Red Guards ransacked temples, museums and offices and persecuted teachers and officials; some 17 million urban youths were 'sent down' to the countryside. Estimates of the death toll range from hundreds of thousands to two million. The movement ended with Mao's death and the arrest of the Gang of Four in 1976.

title.en: Pickles the dog finds the World Cup

lead.en: A collie out for a walk finds the stolen World Cup

summary.en: On 20 March 1966, four months before England hosted the World Cup, the Jules Rimet Trophy was stolen from an exhibition in London. A week later Pickles the collie, out for a walk, found it in the street, wrapped in newspaper. He was invited to England's victory banquet; his owner got about £5,000.

lead.en: The world's largest aircraft skimmed the sea and was a 'ship'

summary.en: Rostislav Alexeyev's ekranoplan, 92 m long and up to 544 tonnes, flew a few metres above the water and from 1966 to 1988 was the largest aircraft in the world. Registered as a ship, it had champagne broken on its nose before its first flight. US intelligence spent years puzzling over the 'monster'.

lead.en: Barnard swaps a heart — the transplant era begins

summary.en: On 3 December 1967 surgeon Christiaan Barnard transplanted a heart into Louis Washkansky at Groote Schuur Hospital; the patient lived 18 days. Drawing partly on experiments by Soviet scientist Vladimir Demikhov, it opened the era of transplant surgery.

lead.en: Biafra's famine is the first beamed into living rooms worldwide

summary.en: On 30 May 1967 Lieutenant Colonel Odumegwu Ojukwu declared the independence of the Igbo-majority Republic of Biafra. Federal forces blockaded it and a terrible famine set in. By various estimates 500,000 to 2 million civilians died, mostly of starvation. Images of dying children shocked the world, and doctors who served in Biafra later founded Médecins Sans Frontières.

lead.en: Israel takes Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank and the Golan

summary.en: From 5 to 10 June 1967 Israel fought Egypt, Syria and Jordan, capturing the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank including East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights. The war's outcome still shapes the Middle East conflict.

title.en: García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude

lead.en: Macondo becomes the peak of magical realism

summary.en: In 1967 Colombian writer Gabriel García Márquez published in Buenos Aires his novel of the Buendía family and the town of Macondo. It became the high point of magical realism and the Latin American Boom, selling tens of millions of copies.

lead.en: A whole country switches to driving on the right overnight

summary.en: On 3 September 1967 Sweden, which drove on the left, switched to the right all at once to match its neighbours. In the early morning traffic stopped, carefully moved across to the other side of the road and set off again. It was the biggest logistical operation in Swedish history.

lead.en: A retired major declares a sea fort his own country

summary.en: In 1967 Paddy Roy Bates ousted a pirate radio station from an abandoned British wartime sea fort 11 km off the coast and declared it the Principality of Sealand. No country recognises the micronation, but it has a flag, an anthem, a currency, passports and a 'princely' family.

lead.en: Dubček's reforms are halted by Warsaw Pact troops

summary.en: In 1968 Czechoslovakia's leadership under Alexander Dubček launched liberal reforms, 'socialism with a human face'. On the night of 20–21 August troops of the USSR and other Warsaw Pact states invaded, and the reforms were reversed.

lead.en: Students build barricades and France grinds to a halt

summary.en: In May 1968 student unrest in the Latin Quarter grew into a general strike by millions of workers. De Gaulle's government survived, but the events transformed French society and culture.

lead.en: Students gunned down ten days before the Olympics

place.en: Plaza of the Three Cultures, Mexico City

summary.en: On 2 October 1968 the army and special units opened fire on a student rally in Mexico City's Plaza of the Three Cultures. The government wanted the protests crushed before the Olympic Games opened on 12 October. Officials reported a few dozen dead, but by various estimates as many as 300 to 400 were killed. The truth was suppressed for decades.

lead.en: Humans set foot on another world for the first time

summary.en: Apollo 11 launched from Cape Canaveral on 16 July 1969, and on 20 July Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first people to walk on the Moon while Michael Collins stayed in orbit. The landing was the climax of the space race.

title.en: Mass deforestation of the Amazon begins

lead.en: A jungle highway opened the way for chainsaws and fires

summary.en: In 1970 Brazil's military government began building the Trans-Amazonian Highway and settling the 'empty' rainforest. Ranchers, loggers and soy farms followed the roads. Since then, by various estimates, about a fifth of the Amazon forest has disappeared. Scientists warn that beyond a tipping point parts of the planet's largest rainforest could turn into savanna.

lead.en: History's deadliest storm, a prelude to Bangladesh's independence

summary.en: On 12 November 1970 the deadliest tropical cyclone on record drove a storm surge into the Ganges delta, killing 300,000 to 500,000 people. Slow relief from West Pakistan fuelled Bengali anger, and a year later the Bangladesh Liberation War began.

lead.en: Brazil keeps the Jules Rimet Trophy for ever

summary.en: On 21 June 1970, in the final at the Estadio Azteca, Brazil beat Italy 4–1. Pelé became the first, and so far only, player to win three World Cups, and Brazil, with its third title, kept the Jules Rimet Trophy for good. It was the first World Cup broadcast in colour, and that Brazil side is often called the greatest ever.

lead.en: The deepest hole on Earth: 12,262 metres down

summary.en: Drilling of borehole SG-3 began on 24 May 1970, and in 1989 it reached 12,262 m, still the deepest hole ever drilled. Heat stopped further progress: about 12 km down it was an unexpected 180 °C, and the mud came up 'boiling' with hydrogen.

lead.en: Nine months of war, and a new nation on the map

summary.en: In March 1971 the Pakistani army launched Operation Searchlight against the Bengali national movement in East Pakistan. Mass killings followed; by various estimates 300,000 to 3 million died, and some 10 million refugees fled to India. In December India entered the war, and on 16 December the Pakistani forces surrendered in Dhaka. Bangladesh was born.

lead.en: A whole CPU on one chip — the road to personal computers

summary.en: In November 1971 Intel released the 4004, the first commercial microprocessor, putting a whole CPU on a single chip with 2,300 transistors. It paved the way for personal computers and ubiquitous digital electronics.

lead.en: An ancient wormwood recipe yields a malaria cure

summary.en: Working in the secret Project 523, chemist Tu Youyou, guided by an ancient Chinese medical text, isolated the antimalarial compound artemisinin from sweet wormwood. Drugs based on it have saved millions of lives, earning her the 2015 Nobel Prize.

lead.en: Jets bomb the presidential palace; Allende dies

summary.en: On 11 September 1973 the military under General Augusto Pinochet overthrew the socialist president Salvador Allende. Jets fired on La Moneda Palace, and Allende took his own life rather than surrender. The US-backed junta ruled for 17 years: more than 3,000 people were killed or disappeared and tens of thousands were imprisoned and tortured. Chile returned to democracy in 1990.

lead.en: An embargo quadruples prices and shakes the West

summary.en: In October 1973, during the Yom Kippur War, Arab oil exporters imposed an embargo on countries supporting Israel. Oil prices roughly quadrupled, hitting Western economies and revealing the power of oil-producing states.

lead.en: Utzon's sails become the symbol of Australia

summary.en: On 20 October 1973 Queen Elizabeth II opened Danish architect Jørn Utzon's building with its sail-like roof shells. It became the symbol of Australia and one of the masterpieces of 20th-century architecture, now a World Heritage Site.

title.en: The fall of the Tree of Ténéré

lead.en: A truck hits the only tree for hundreds of kilometres

summary.en: This lone acacia in the Sahara was a landmark for caravans, marked even on 1:4,000,000 maps. It stood for about 300 years until 1973, when it was knocked down by a truck whose driver was reportedly drunk. A metal sculpture now stands in its place.

lead.en: A 3.2-million-year-old skeleton shows ancestors walked upright

summary.en: On 24 November 1974 palaeoanthropologists Donald Johanson and Tom Gray found about 40% of the skeleton of an australopithecine that lived 3.2 million years ago in Ethiopia's Afar desert. Her pelvis and legs showed that Australopithecus afarensis already walked upright, though its brain was ape-sized. She was named Lucy after a Beatles song playing in camp; in Ethiopia she is Dinkinesh, 'you are marvellous'.

lead.en: Its inventor needed a month to solve his own puzzle

summary.en: In 1974 Hungarian architecture lecturer Ernő Rubik built his 'Magic Cube' as a teaching aid. After scrambling it for the first time, he needed about a month to solve it himself. Some 500 million have since been sold, making it the best-selling toy in the world.

lead.en: A Japanese officer fights on 29 years after the war

summary.en: Lieutenant Hiroo Onoda dismissed leaflets and family letters saying the war was over and fought on in the jungles of Lubang. He agreed to surrender only in March 1974, when his former commander, by then a bookseller, flew in from Japan to give the order in person: 10,416 days after Japan's surrender.

title.en: The Khmer Rouge and the Cambodian genocide

lead.en: 'Year Zero': a capital emptied within days

summary.en: On 17 April 1975 Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge entered Phnom Penh and within days drove its entire population into the countryside. Money, schools and religion were abolished, and 'class enemies' and the educated were killed; thousands were tortured to death in the S-21 prison. By estimates 1.5 to 2 million Cambodians died, nearly a quarter of the population. The regime fell to a Vietnamese invasion in January 1979.

lead.en: Sectarian war wrecks the 'Switzerland of the East' for 15 years

summary.en: On 13 April 1975 Phalangist gunmen fired on a bus carrying Palestinians in Beirut's Ain el-Remmaneh district, and the country slid into war among Christian, Muslim, Druze and Palestinian militias. Syria and Israel intervened; in 1982 the Israeli army besieged Beirut. An estimated 120,000–150,000 people were killed. The war ended with the 1989 Taif Agreement and final fighting in October 1990.

lead.en: Three languages aboard: Russian, English and 'Oklahomski'

summary.en: On 17 July 1975 Soyuz and Apollo docked and Leonov shook hands with Stafford. NASA had expected the handshake over the English resort of Bognor Regis; a delay put it over Metz in France. Teasing Stafford's drawl, Leonov said three languages were spoken: Russian, English and 'Oklahomski'.

lead.en: A night tremor flattens an industrial city in seconds

summary.en: On 28 July 1976 a night-time earthquake levelled the industrial city of Tangshan in seconds; the official death toll was about 242,000, and other estimates are higher. The government refused foreign aid. Six weeks later, Mao Zedong died.

title.en: Last traces of the Javan tiger

lead.en: A crowded island leaves no room for its big cat

summary.en: In 1976 tracks of a few tigers found in the Meru Betiri reserve were the last reliable evidence of the Javan subspecies, later declared extinct. Java, one of the world's most crowded islands, left no room for the predator, and the related Bali tiger had vanished too.

lead.en: No compass, no charts: only stars, swells and birds

summary.en: In 1976 the double-hulled canoe Hōkūleʻa, built on ancient lines, sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti, some 4,000 km, without a single navigation instrument. It was guided by Mau Piailug of Satawal atoll in Micronesia, one of the last keepers of traditional wayfinding. The voyage undercut the theory that Polynesia was settled by accidental drift and spurred the Hawaiian cultural renaissance.

lead.en: Lucas's space saga launches the blockbuster era

summary.en: On 25 May 1977 George Lucas's space saga opened in cinemas. It became the highest-grossing film to that date, revolutionised visual effects and ushered in the era of blockbusters and a vast media franchise.

lead.en: The guillotine is still in use in the year of Star Wars

summary.en: On 10 September 1977 Hamida Djandoubi was guillotined in Marseille's Baumettes prison, the last execution in France and in Western Europe. France abolished the death penalty in 1981.

lead.en: A message to aliens: Bach, whales and Chuck Berry

summary.en: In 1977 both Voyagers carried gilded records for any aliens: greetings in 55 languages, whale songs, laughter, Bach, Mozart and Chuck Berry's 'Johnny B. Goode'. When a folklorist objected that rock was adolescent, Carl Sagan replied: 'There are a lot of adolescents on the planet.'

lead.en: 72 seconds from space that never came back

summary.en: On 15 August 1977 the Big Ear radio telescope picked up a strong narrowband signal from Sagittarius lasting 72 seconds. Astronomer Jerry Ehman circled the readout and wrote 'Wow!' in the margin. Decades of searching have never found it again.

lead.en: Markets and opening-up launch China's decades of growth

summary.en: In December 1978 a Communist Party plenum led by Deng Xiaoping launched the policy of reform and opening-up. Market mechanisms, foreign investment and special economic zones gave China decades of rapid growth and made it one of the world's largest economies.

lead.en: Egypt becomes the first Arab state to make peace with Israel

summary.en: On 17 September 1978, after 13 days of talks at the US presidential retreat, Egypt's Anwar Sadat and Israel's Menachem Begin signed framework accords brokered by Jimmy Carter. Under the 1979 peace treaty Israel returned Sinai to Egypt by 1982. Sadat and Begin shared the Nobel Peace Prize, but Egypt was suspended from the Arab League for a decade, and Sadat was assassinated in 1981.

lead.en: The shah leaves and Khomeini takes the helm

summary.en: Mass protests forced Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi to leave Iran in January 1979. Ayatollah Khomeini returned from exile to lead the country, and after a referendum Iran was declared an Islamic Republic. The revolution reshaped the balance of power in the Middle East.

lead.en: The USSR fights the mujahideen for nearly a decade

summary.en: In December 1979 Soviet troops entered Afghanistan to support its pro-Soviet government and fought the mujahideen. The withdrawal was completed in February 1989; Soviet losses were about 15,000 killed.

lead.en: For the first time, humanity wipes out a disease

summary.en: On 8 May 1980 the World Health Assembly declared smallpox eradicated, the first human disease ever wiped out. The WHO's global vaccination drive had been proposed by the USSR in 1958; the last natural case was found in Somalia in 1977.

lead.en: A mountainside collapses in the largest landslide ever recorded

summary.en: On 18 May 1980 the volcano's north flank collapsed in the largest landslide ever recorded, and a lateral blast flattened forest over 600 km². Fifty-seven people died, including volcanologist David Johnston. It became one of the most studied eruptions in the world.

lead.en: A shipyard strike sparks the movement that ends Polish communism

summary.en: In August 1980 a strike at the Gdańsk Shipyard led by Lech Wałęsa produced Solidarity, the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc. With some 10 million members, it was central to the fall of communism in Poland in 1989.

lead.en: Eight years of trench warfare, and the border stayed put

summary.en: On 22 September 1980 Saddam Hussein invaded Iran, counting on post-revolutionary chaos. The war became an attritional slaughter of human-wave attacks, strikes on cities and tankers, and Iraqi use of chemical weapons. By various estimates hundreds of thousands died. In August 1988 both sides accepted UN Resolution 598 and a ceasefire.

lead.en: First report of a disease that would kill over 40 million

summary.en: On 5 June 1981 a bulletin from the US Centers for Disease Control described a rare pneumonia in five young men in Los Angeles — the first report of the disease later named AIDS. In 1983 French scientists isolated the virus behind it, HIV, which had passed to humans from chimpanzees in Central Africa in the early 20th century. UNAIDS estimates that over 40 million people have died of AIDS-related illnesses.

title.en: Birth of the Internet: ARPANET adopts TCP/IP

lead.en: One common language links networks into a global web

summary.en: On 1 January 1983 ARPANET, funded by the US defence research agency, switched entirely to Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn's TCP/IP protocols. A common language for linking different networks became the foundation of the global Internet.

lead.en: A BBC report gives birth to Band Aid and Live Aid

summary.en: Drought in northern Ethiopia combined with civil war and the policies of the Derg military regime, which blocked aid to rebel areas and forcibly resettled peasants. By various estimates 300,000 to 1.2 million people died. Michael Buerk's report from the Korem camp in October 1984 shocked the West, inspiring the Band Aid single and the Live Aid concert, which raised tens of millions of dollars.

lead.en: −89.2 °C, the lowest reliably measured temperature on Earth

summary.en: On 21 July 1983 the Soviet Antarctic station Vostok, founded in 1957, recorded −89.2 °C, the lowest temperature ever reliably measured on Earth. Beneath the station, under almost four kilometres of ice, lies the huge subglacial Lake Vostok.

lead.en: The worst industrial disaster ever struck as a city slept

summary.en: On the night of 2–3 December 1984 about 40 tonnes of toxic methyl isocyanate leaked from the American firm Union Carbide's pesticide plant. The gas cloud settled over the sleeping slums around the factory. The official toll in the first days was 2,259 dead, while by various estimates total deaths exceeded 15,000; more than half a million people were injured.

lead.en: Falling blocks from Moscow conquer the world

summary.en: In June 1984 Alexey Pajitnov, a programmer at the Soviet Academy of Sciences' Computing Centre, wrote a game of falling blocks on an Elektronika 60 computer. Tetris became one of the most popular video games ever made.

lead.en: Gorbachev launches glasnost and sweeping reforms

summary.en: In March 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev became General Secretary of the Communist Party and launched perestroika and glasnost. The reforms eased censorship and introduced contested elections and market elements, amid a deepening economic crisis.

lead.en: CFCs thin the ozone over Antarctica and the world responds

summary.en: In 1985 British Antarctic Survey scientists, using years of data from Halley station, reported a sharp springtime loss of ozone over Antarctica. CFCs were to blame, and by 1987 nations had signed the Montreal Protocol to protect the ozone layer.

title.en: The sinking of the Rainbow Warrior

lead.en: French spies bombed a Greenpeace ship in a foreign port

summary.en: On the night of 10 July 1985 two mines sank Greenpeace's flagship in Auckland harbour as it prepared to sail to Moruroa to protest French nuclear tests. Photographer Fernando Pereira was killed. New Zealand police soon caught two agents of the French DGSE, and the scandal cost Defence Minister Charles Hernu his post. New Zealand hardened its nuclear-free stance.

lead.en: The worst nuclear power accident empties Pripyat

summary.en: On 26 April 1986 an explosion at reactor No. 4 of the Chernobyl plant caused the worst accident in the history of nuclear power. Radioactive fallout spread across much of Europe, the town of Pripyat was evacuated and an exclusion zone was created around the plant.

title.en: Mathias Rust lands by Red Square

lead.en: An 18-year-old amateur pilot slips through Soviet air defence

summary.en: On 28 May 1987, Border Guards Day, Mathias Rust, a German with about 50 hours of flying, left Helsinki in a rented Cessna and landed on a bridge by Red Square. Defence Minister Sokolov and hundreds of officers were sacked, and Muscovites nicknamed the square 'Sheremetyevo-3'.

title.en: Invention of the World Wide Web

lead.en: Berners-Lee links documents with hypertext

summary.en: In 1989 British scientist Tim Berners-Lee at CERN proposed a system of hypertext documents linked over the internet. Opened to the public in 1991, the World Wide Web turned the internet, which grew out of the US ARPANET, into a global medium.

lead.en: The border opens as the Cold War draws to a close

summary.en: On 9 November 1989 East German authorities opened the border, and Berliners poured through the wall that had divided the city since 1961. Its fall became the symbol of the end of the Cold War and led to German reunification in October 1990.

lead.en: Communist regimes fall one after another, mostly peacefully

summary.en: In 1989 communist regimes fell in Poland, Hungary, East Germany, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia (the Velvet Revolution) and Romania. Except in Romania, the changes were largely peaceful and led to multiparty elections.

lead.en: The army ends the protest and political reform stalls

summary.en: For weeks students and workers occupied Beijing's main square demanding free speech and an end to corruption. On the night of 4 June the army crushed the protest; hundreds, perhaps thousands, were killed and political reform in China was halted.

title.en: Last sighting of the golden toad

lead.en: Monteverde's bright amphibian vanishes amid drought and fungus

summary.en: On 15 May 1989 the last male of the bright orange golden toad, found only on a few square kilometres, was seen in Monteverde's cloud forest. Drought and a fungal disease of amphibians are blamed. The species is now listed as extinct; that year, the Berlin Wall fell.

lead.en: A 675-km human chain links three nations seeking independence

summary.en: On 23 August 1989, the 50th anniversary of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, about two million people in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania joined hands in a 675 km human chain. The three republics declared independence in 1990–1991.

title.en: Launch of the Hubble Space Telescope

lead.en: An eye in orbit refines the age of the universe

summary.en: On 24 April 1990 Space Shuttle Discovery carried the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit. Once its flawed mirror was corrected in 1993, it helped pin down the age of the universe and discover its accelerating expansion.

lead.en: Hundreds of burning oil wells and a 100-hour ground war

summary.en: On 2 August 1990 Iraq seized Kuwait. A UN-mandated coalition of more than 30 countries led by the United States launched Operation Desert Storm in January 1991: five weeks of air strikes and a 100-hour ground offensive. Retreating Iraqi troops set hundreds of Kuwaiti oil wells ablaze; the fires burned until November 1991.

lead.en: East Germany joins the West — Germany is one again

summary.en: On 3 October 1990, less than a year after the fall of the Berlin Wall, the German Democratic Republic joined the Federal Republic. Reunification was preceded by the Two Plus Four Treaty with the USSR, the United States, Britain and France. Soviet troops left Germany by 1994.

lead.en: Fifteen independent states emerge from the Union

summary.en: In December 1991 the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus signed the Belovezha Accords, and on 25 December Mikhail Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president. Fifteen independent states emerged in place of the USSR, and the Cold War came to an end.

lead.en: Forecasts save tens of thousands; the planet cools half a degree

summary.en: On 15 June 1991 came the second-largest eruption of the 20th century. Forecasts allowed tens of thousands to be evacuated, but a passing typhoon turned the ash into heavy mud that collapsed roofs. Global temperatures fell by about half a degree for two years.

lead.en: Yugoslavia's break-up brings war and ethnic cleansing

summary.en: In 1991 Slovenia and Croatia left Yugoslavia, followed by Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina; the break-up brought wars in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo. The siege of Sarajevo lasted almost four years, and about 8,000 Bosniak Muslims were killed at Srebrenica in 1995. Some 130,000–140,000 people died in all.

lead.en: A failed bid to oust Gorbachev hastens the Soviet collapse

summary.en: On 19–21 August 1991 hardliners of the State Emergency Committee tried to oust Gorbachev and block a new union treaty. Resistance led by Boris Yeltsin at the Moscow White House defeated the coup and hastened the end of the USSR.

lead.en: Twelve states create the EU and set a path to the euro

summary.en: Twelve member states of the European Communities signed the treaty creating the European Union. It introduced EU citizenship and a common foreign policy and set the path to a single currency, the euro.

lead.en: A court ruled Australia was never "nobody's land"

place.en: Mer Island, Torres Strait, and Canberra

summary.en: On 3 June 1992 the High Court of Australia ruled six to one against the doctrine of terra nullius, under which the continent had been treated as belonging to no one before the British. The case was brought by Eddie Koiki Mabo of Mer Island in the Torres Strait, defending his family's land. He died months before the verdict. The ruling led to the Native Title Act of 1993.

title.en: Living in Bondage and the birth of Nollywood

lead.en: A straight-to-video hit launches Nigeria's film industry

summary.en: Shot on video and sold on cassettes, the Nigerian film Living in Bondage became a hit and proved films could be made cheaply and fast. It launched Nollywood, one of the world's largest film industries by output.

lead.en: Israel and the PLO recognise each other for the first time

summary.en: After secret talks in Norway, Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization signed a Declaration of Principles at the White House on 13 September 1993, sealed by a handshake between Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat. The two sides recognised each other and the Palestinian Authority was created. Core issues — borders, Jerusalem, refugees, settlements — were deferred; in 1995 Rabin was assassinated by an Israeli opponent of the accords.

title.en: Adoption of the Constitution of Russia

lead.en: A national vote establishes a presidential republic

summary.en: After the constitutional crisis of September–October 1993, which ended with the shelling of the Supreme Soviet building, a new constitution was adopted by referendum on 12 December. It established a presidential republic.

title.en: End of apartheid in South Africa

lead.en: The first all-race election makes Mandela president

summary.en: In April 1994 South Africa held its first elections open to citizens of all races. Nelson Mandela, who had spent 27 years in prison, became president. It ended apartheid, the decades-long system of racial segregation.

lead.en: About a hundred days of mass killing, mostly of Tutsi

summary.en: Over about a hundred days from April to July 1994, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly Tutsi as well as moderate Hutu, were killed in Rwanda. The world's failure to stop the killings became a grave lesson for the United Nations.

lead.en: An adult animal copied — the world debates human cloning

summary.en: On 5 July 1996 Dolly the sheep was born at the Roslin Institute, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. Her announcement in 1997 sparked worldwide debate about human cloning.

lead.en: Britain's last major colony returns to China

summary.en: At midnight on 1 July 1997 Britain handed Hong Kong to China after 156 years of rule. Under the 1984 Joint Declaration the city was to keep its own laws, currency and economy for 50 years under 'one country, two systems'. For London it symbolically closed the empire in Asia; since the 2020 national security law, the city's autonomy has narrowed markedly.

lead.en: A machine beats a reigning world champion for the first time

summary.en: On 11 May 1997 IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov 3½–2½. It was the first time a computer defeated a reigning world champion in a match under classical time controls.

lead.en: India and Pakistan go openly nuclear

summary.en: On 11 and 13 May 1998 India carried out five underground nuclear tests at Pokhran in the Thar Desert. Two weeks later, on 28 and 30 May, Pakistan responded with tests in the Chagai Hills of Balochistan. The US and others imposed sanctions, but both countries have since openly maintained nuclear arsenals, and every crisis between them alarms the world.

lead.en: 'Africa's World War', with deaths in the millions

summary.en: In August 1998 Rwanda and Uganda backed a rebellion against their former ally, Congo's President Laurent-Désiré Kabila, while Angola, Zimbabwe and Namibia came to his defence. Nine African countries and dozens of armed groups, many fighting over mines, were drawn in. The International Rescue Committee estimated 5.4 million excess deaths from 1998 to 2007, mostly from hunger and disease; other researchers consider this too high.

title.en: Launch of the International Space Station

lead.en: The Zarya module begins a shared home in orbit

summary.en: On 20 November 1998 the Zarya module, the first component of the International Space Station, launched from Baikonur. The station is a partnership of the space agencies of Russia, the US, Europe, Japan and Canada, and has been continuously crewed since 2000.

title.en: Death of the last Pyrenean ibex

lead.en: A lost species is cloned — and goes extinct a second time

summary.en: On 6 January 2000 a falling tree killed Celia, the last Pyrenean ibex, or bucardo, in the Spanish Pyrenees. In 2003 a clone was born from her cells but lived only minutes: the first 'de-extinction' in history, and the first second extinction.

lead.en: Yeltsin's successor wins the election in the first round

summary.en: After Boris Yeltsin resigned on 31 December 1999, Vladimir Putin became acting president. On 26 March 2000 he won the election in the first round with 53% of the vote and took office on 7 May.

lead.en: Hijacked planes strike New York and the Pentagon

summary.en: On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four airliners, flying two into the World Trade Center towers and one into the Pentagon; the fourth crashed in Pennsylvania. Nearly 3,000 people were killed. The attacks led the US to launch the War on Terror, including the war in Afghanistan.

lead.en: America's longest war ends with the Taliban back in power

summary.en: On 7 October 2001, after the 9/11 attacks and the Taliban's refusal to hand over Osama bin Laden, the US and its allies began strikes on Afghanistan; by December the Taliban regime had fallen. But an insurgency dragged on for twenty years. Under a 2020 deal the US began withdrawing, and on 15 August 2021, before the pullout was complete, the Taliban entered Kabul. The Costs of War project estimates over 170,000 deaths in Afghanistan.

lead.en: China becomes the workshop of the world

summary.en: On 11 December 2001, after 15 years of talks, China joined the World Trade Organization. Lower tariffs and secure access to world markets fuelled a boom: exports grew more than fivefold from 2001 to 2008, and in 2009 China became the world's largest exporter. The flood of cheap goods hit manufacturing jobs in the US and Europe.

lead.en: Twelve countries swap francs, marks and lire for one currency

summary.en: On 1 January 2002 euro notes and coins entered circulation in twelve EU countries; the non-cash euro had existed since 1999. National currencies were withdrawn within two months.

lead.en: A map of 3 billion DNA letters opens genomic medicine

summary.en: In April 2003 the international Human Genome Project, begun in 1990, announced it had sequenced essentially the whole human genome. The map of some 3 billion DNA letters opened the way to genetic diagnosis and personalised medicine.

lead.en: A US-led coalition topples Saddam Hussein

summary.en: In March 2003 a US-led coalition invaded Iraq and overthrew Saddam Hussein; the weapons of mass destruction cited as the main reason for war were never found. Years of violence and instability followed, and US troops left in 2011.

lead.en: Waves strike 14 countries, leaving about 230,000 dead

summary.en: On 26 December 2004 a magnitude 9.1–9.3 earthquake off Sumatra sent tsunamis onto the coasts of 14 countries, from Indonesia and Thailand to Sri Lanka and Somalia. About 230,000 people died, including thousands of tourists. A warning system for the ocean followed.

lead.en: The first whale or dolphin lost to human activity

summary.en: In 2006 an expedition surveyed thousands of kilometres of the Yangtze and found no baiji, a river dolphin that had lived there for millions of years. It was declared functionally extinct, killed by fishing nets, shipping and dams: the first cetacean wiped out by humans.

lead.en: Touchscreen and web in a pocket — the smartphone age

summary.en: On 9 January 2007 Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone, a phone with a large multi-touch screen and a full web browser. Smartphones soon became the main device for communication, media and work for billions of people.

lead.en: Lehman Brothers' collapse plunges the world into recession

summary.en: Turmoil in the US subprime mortgage market became a global crisis after the investment bank Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008. Governments rescued banks with trillions of dollars, and the world economy suffered its deepest downturn since the Great Depression.

lead.en: Australia formally apologises for taking Aboriginal children

summary.en: On 13 February 2008 Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologised on behalf of Parliament to the Stolen Generations — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children removed from their families by authorities from the early 20th century into the 1970s. A 1997 report found that between one in ten and one in three Indigenous children had been taken. The previous government of John Howard had refused to apologise.

lead.en: A quake levels the capital of the Americas' poorest country

summary.en: On 12 January 2010 a magnitude 7.0 earthquake centred near Léogâne destroyed much of Port-au-Prince. The death toll is uncertain, with estimates from 100,000 to over 300,000, and about 1.5 million people lost their homes. That autumn a cholera epidemic broke out, traced by researchers to UN peacekeepers; it killed nearly 10,000 people.

lead.en: A protest in Tunisia sparks uprisings across the region

summary.en: The self-immolation of street vendor Mohamed Bouazizi in Sidi Bouzid, Tunisia, in December 2010 sparked protests across the Arab world. The rulers of Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen were toppled, and civil wars broke out in Libya, Syria and Yemen.

lead.en: 828 metres: Dubai builds the tallest structure on Earth

summary.en: On 4 January 2010 Dubai opened an 828-metre skyscraper, the tallest structure in the world. Construction took six years; amid a debt crisis Abu Dhabi bailed the emirate out, and the tower, planned as Burj Dubai, was named after UAE President Khalifa bin Zayed. It became the symbol of a fishing town's transformation into a global metropolis.

lead.en: Waves cripple Fukushima: worst nuclear crisis since Chernobyl

summary.en: On 11 March 2011 Japan's strongest recorded earthquake, magnitude 9.0–9.1, unleashed tsunamis up to 40 m high; about 18,000 people died or went missing. The wave crippled the Fukushima Daiichi plant, causing the worst nuclear accident since Chernobyl.

lead.en: Peaceful protests turn into a war drawing in world powers

summary.en: In March 2011 protests broke out in Daraa; Bashar al-Assad's government met them with force, and by 2012 the confrontation had become a war. Iran, Hezbollah, Russia, Turkey, the US and its allies intervened, and the Islamic State rose amid the chaos. Estimates of the dead range from about 500,000 to over 600,000, and about half the pre-war population fled their homes. Assad's government fell in December 2024.

lead.en: The collider finds the Standard Model's missing piece

summary.en: On 4 July 2012 CERN physicists announced that the Large Hadron Collider had found a particle predicted almost 50 years earlier. The Higgs boson completed the Standard Model, earning Peter Higgs and François Englert the Nobel Prize.

lead.en: Pinta's last tortoise, a global symbol of extinction, dies

summary.en: On 24 June 2012 Lonesome George, the last tortoise from Pinta Island, died in the Galápagos. Found in 1971, he spent 40 years as scientists searched in vain for a mate of his own kind. He became a global symbol of vanishing species.

lead.en: A GPU-trained network kicks off the modern AI boom

summary.en: In 2012 a neural network by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, trained on graphics cards, won a major image-recognition contest by a huge margin. Its success launched the deep-learning boom behind modern AI.
